title: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHY DID HE SAY HE DIDN’T KNOW WHEN HE WOULD RETURN?
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHY DID HE SAY HE DIDN’T KNOW WHEN HE WOULD RETURN?
One Sentence That Seems to Contradict His Divinity—Until You Discover What Happened When the Eternal Son Stepped Into Human Flesh.

There is a question that has shaken the faith of sincere Christians, fueled countless debates, and given skeptics what they believe is one of their strongest arguments against the divinity of Jesus Christ.
And the unsettling part?
The question comes from the mouth of Jesus Himself.
Not from an atheist. Not from a false teacher. Not from someone trying to discredit Christianity.
From Jesus.
He was sitting on the Mount of Olives, speaking about the future, the coming judgment, and the day when the Son of Man would come in power and glory.
Then He said something extraordinary.
“But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.” — Mark 13:32 (KJV)
Read those last words again.
Neither the Son.
Wait.
If Jesus is truly God, and God knows everything, how could Jesus say He did not know the day or hour of His return?
Was He admitting that He was not God?
Was He somehow less divine than the Father?
Or is there something about the incarnation that many Christians have never fully understood?

Because buried inside this difficult question is a truth so breathtaking that it takes us from the throne of heaven to the dust of Bethlehem, from the glory of eternity to the humiliation of the cross, and from our deepest human weakness to the astonishing grace of God.
And when you begin to understand it, you may never read Philippians 2 the same way again.
But first, we must do something many people avoid.
We must allow the difficult words of Jesus to remain difficult.
We must not twist Scripture to protect a doctrine.
The truth of Jesus Christ does not need protection from the words of Jesus Christ.
It needs careful understanding.
And the journey begins with a single Greek sentence.
In Mark 13:32, the original Greek includes these words:
οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
Oude ho huios, ei mē ho patēr.
A faithful translation is:
“Nor the Son, except the Father.”
The Greek expression οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός really does mean “nor the Son.”
There is no hidden grammatical trick that makes the statement disappear.
Jesus truly said it.
And that matters.
Because biblical faith is not built by pretending uncomfortable verses do not exist.
It is built by listening to everything God has revealed.
John tells us that the Word was with God and that the Word was God (John 1:1). He then declares that this same Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
Thomas looked upon the risen Jesus and cried, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).
Paul describes Christ as the One in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9).
And Hebrews speaks of the Son in language of divine glory, creation, and eternal sovereignty (Hebrews 1:2–3, 8–12).
Yet Mark records Jesus saying that the Son did not know the hour.
These passages are not competing voices that we are free to silence whenever one becomes inconvenient.
They are all part of the testimony of Scripture.
So how do we hold them together?
We begin by understanding something Christianity has confessed for centuries.
Jesus Christ is not half God and half man. He is truly God and truly man.
Not two separate persons.
Not a divine being merely pretending to be human.
Not an ordinary man who eventually became God.
He is the eternal Son of God who assumed a complete human nature without ceasing to be divine.
One Person, two natures.
Fully divine.
Fully human.
And suddenly, the question becomes much deeper than whether Jesus possessed divine knowledge.
It becomes a question about what it meant for the eternal Son to enter our human condition.
Imagine the scene.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world as a baby.
The One who sustains creation was carried in His mother's arms.
The One who gives life experienced hunger.
The One who created the seas became thirsty.
The One whom angels worship grew tired enough to sleep in a boat.
And the One who is life itself willingly submitted to death.
This is not a contradiction of His divinity.
This is the staggering mystery of His incarnation.
Luke tells us that Jesus grew in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:52).
Think about that.
He grew in wisdom.
That is not how we would describe a merely disguised deity pretending to experience childhood.
That is how Scripture describes a real human life.
Jesus did not simply wear humanity like a costume.
He truly became man.
He knew what it was to grow, learn, suffer, become weary, and live in dependence upon the Father.
And this is where Philippians 2 becomes essential.
Paul writes:
The Greek is remarkable.
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
Heauton ekenōsen.
Literally:
“He emptied Himself.”
That word, ekenōsen, comes from the Greek verb kenoō, meaning to empty or make empty.
But what exactly did Jesus empty Himself of?
His divinity?
His eternal existence?
His divine nature?
No.
And here is where we must be extremely careful.
Philippians 2 does not say Jesus stopped being God.
It does not say He discarded His divine attributes or became a lesser deity.
The passage explains His self-emptying through what follows: He took the form of a servant and was born in human likeness.
The eternal Son humbled Himself, not by abandoning deity, but by assuming genuine humanity and entering the lowliness of servanthood.
He did not cease to be what He eternally was.
He became what He had not previously been.
Human.
The One who was equal with God did not cling to the privileges of His exalted position for selfish advantage.
Instead, He entered a world of pain, rejection, temptation, suffering, and death.
Not because He had lost His divine identity.
But because He had come to save people who could never save themselves.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is this:
He did not come merely to experience humanity.
He came to redeem it.
Now return to Mark 13:32.
When Jesus said that the Son did not know the day or hour, He was speaking during His earthly ministry, in the reality of His incarnate human life.
In historic Christian theology, His human nature included a genuinely human mind and human experience.
And a genuinely human mind is not automatically identical to the infinite divine knowledge belonging to the divine nature.
This distinction is important.
The eternal Son remains omniscient in His deity.
Yet in His earthly human life, Scripture presents Him as growing in wisdom and, in Mark 13:32, acknowledging that He did not know the appointed hour.
That is not the same as saying His divine nature became ignorant.
Nor does it mean Jesus was two persons, one knowing and another speaking.
It means the one divine Person truly lived a human life.
Christians have expressed the relationship between Christ's divine knowledge and human knowledge in different ways, and Scripture does not explain every detail of that mystery.
Some emphasize that Jesus did not exercise or communicate divine knowledge independently during His earthly mission. Others emphasize the genuine limitations of His human knowledge.
What we must not do is claim that the Greek word for “know” secretly means “reveal” in Mark 13:32.
That interpretation is sometimes suggested, but it is not the ordinary meaning of the text and should not be presented as a proven solution.
Jesus said He did not know.
Our responsibility is to take His words seriously while also taking seriously the full biblical testimony to His deity.
And there is another detail worth noticing.
In the same chapter, Jesus describes the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory (Mark 13:26).
He speaks of gathering His elect (Mark 13:27).
He warns His disciples to remain watchful.
The point of His teaching is not to provide a mathematical formula for the end of history.
It is to call His people to faithful readiness.
Jesus is not inviting His followers to become obsessed with discovering a date He did not disclose.
He is commanding them to live in such a way that they are ready whenever He comes.
And that brings us to something deeply personal.
Because many of us have spent more time asking when Jesus will return than asking whether our lives reflect the Jesus who is returning.
We want to understand prophecy.
But do we obey His commands?
We want to identify the signs.
But have we repented of the sins we keep excusing?
We want to know what happens at the end of the world.
But what is happening inside our hearts right now?
We can debate the Greek text, study the chronology, compare interpretations, and defend the doctrine of the incarnation.
Those are worthwhile things when done faithfully.
But knowledge about Christ must never become a substitute for knowing Christ.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not ignorance.
It is the ability to explain sacred truths while resisting the Lord those truths reveal.
You can defend the deity of Jesus in a comment section and still refuse to surrender your bitterness to Him.
You can argue passionately about the Second Coming while neglecting the people He has commanded you to love.
You can know the theological meaning of kenosis and still be unwilling to humble yourself before God.
And if that stings, perhaps it is because this question is no longer merely about Mark 13:32.
Perhaps it has become a question about us.
What are we doing with the Jesus we claim to believe in?
Because the One who humbled Himself did not call us merely to admire His humility.
He called us to follow Him.
Paul introduces the teaching of Philippians 2 with a command:
“Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.” — Philippians 2:5 (KJV)
Do you see it?
Paul did not write these words merely to satisfy intellectual curiosity about the incarnation.
He was urging believers to abandon selfish ambition, embrace humility, and care for one another.
The theology was meant to transform the way they lived.
The eternal Son humbled Himself.
And we struggle to apologize.
He took the form of a servant.
And we fight to be recognized.
He endured rejection.
And we sometimes abandon obedience the moment following Him becomes uncomfortable.
He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
And we hesitate to surrender the very sins from which He came to deliver us.
This is not written to crush the struggling believer.
It is written to awaken us to the beauty and seriousness of the Gospel.
Because the story does not end with our failures.
It never did.
The cross is where our rebellion meets the mercy of God.
Listen to the rest of Paul's words:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” — Philippians 2:8 (KJV)
There it is.
The destination of His humiliation.
Not merely Bethlehem.
Not merely the carpenter's workshop.
Not merely the dusty roads of Galilee.
Calvary.
The eternal Son entered our humanity to accomplish what fallen humanity could never accomplish for itself.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He suffered without sin.
He offered Himself for sinners.
And He rose again in victory.
His humanity was not a weakness that ruined God's plan.
It was essential to the saving mission He willingly undertook.

Hebrews tells us that because the children share in flesh and blood, Christ likewise partook of the same, so that through death He might defeat the one who held the power of death and deliver those enslaved by fear (Hebrews 2:14–15).
And Hebrews 4:15 reminds us that our High Priest can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Think about what that means for the person reading this who feels completely exhausted.
The person whose prayers have become whispers.
The person who smiles in church but cries alone at night.
The person who has failed again and wonders whether God has finally become tired of forgiving them.
The person who knows all the right Christian language but feels spiritually empty.
Jesus is not a distant Savior who merely observed human suffering from heaven.
He entered our world.
He knew hunger.
He knew weariness.
He knew sorrow.
He knew betrayal.
He knew the agony of suffering.
And He remained perfectly faithful.
That does not mean He experienced every particular hardship you have faced.
It means He is a genuinely human, sinless, compassionate High Priest who is able to help those who come to Him.
You do not have to pretend your weakness is invisible to Him.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance before approaching His throne.
You are invited to come boldly to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this tonight:
The Jesus who entered human weakness is not ashamed to receive a broken sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
He does not excuse the darkness.
He brings us out of it.
He does not call evil good.
He forgives, cleanses, and transforms those who turn to Him.
He does not merely rewrite our public reputation.
He changes our relationship with God.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because our past never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin always disappear.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue in rebellion.
But because Jesus Christ died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
And now, consider one final detail about the day and hour.
After His resurrection, the disciples asked Jesus about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel.
He answered:
“It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.” — Acts 1:7 (KJV)
Notice the emphasis.
He did not give them a date.
He redirected their attention to their calling.
In the very next verse, He promised that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them and that they would be His witnesses (Acts 1:8).
The disciples wanted a timetable.
Jesus gave them a mission.
And perhaps we need that correction too.
We do not know when He will return.
We do know that He has called us to repent, believe the Gospel, love one another, make disciples, and bear witness to His truth.
We do not know the appointed hour.
We do know that every hour is an opportunity to walk faithfully with Him.
We do not know how many more opportunities we will have to speak to someone we love about Jesus.
But we know the message entrusted to us.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And salvation is found in Him.
That is why the question, “If Jesus is God, why did He say He did not know the day or hour?” should not drive us away from Christ.
It should drive us deeper into the mystery and wonder of who He is.
The eternal Son did not stop being God when He became man.
He truly entered our humanity.
And in that humanity, He humbled Himself all the way to the cross.
But the cross was not the end.
Paul continues:
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.” — Philippians 2:9 (KJV)
The One who humbled Himself has been exalted.
The One who was crucified is risen.
The One who was rejected will be confessed as Lord.
And the One who promised to return will fulfill His promise.
We cannot calculate the day.
We cannot command the hour.
We cannot force the mysteries of the incarnation into a simple slogan that answers every philosophical question.
But we can worship the One whom Scripture reveals.
We can trust His saving work.
We can obey His Word.
And we can live ready.
Maybe you began reading this article looking for an argument to settle a theological debate.
But perhaps, somewhere along the way, another question began stirring inside you.
If Jesus humbled Himself so completely to save sinners, why am I still holding back the part of my life I know He is calling me to surrender?
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is a secret habit.
Maybe it is unforgiveness.
Maybe it is the exhausting effort of appearing spiritually strong when you are barely holding on.
Whatever it is, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The call to repentance is not an announcement that grace is unavailable.
It is an invitation to stop running from the Savior who is able to forgive and restore.
Turn to Him.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Trust what He accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And ask Him to teach you to walk in the newness of life He gives.

You do not have to disclose your private struggles publicly. A sincere prayer request is enough. And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from shame into forgiveness and a changed life, your words may encourage someone who believes their story is beyond redemption.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass someone with questions.

But because there may be a struggling believer, a skeptical friend, a family member, or someone quietly walking away from Christianity who has never heard this passage explained with both biblical honesty and compassion.

We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not silenced, biblical truth is not compromised, repentance is not forgotten, and the grace of Jesus Christ is never reduced to an empty religious slogan.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not be able to afford paid materials.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another way you can participate in its mission.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful rather than forced or pressured (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That distinction matters deeply to us.
These are small expressions of thanks.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
We want to see people reading their Bibles again.
Families praying together again.
Wounded believers finding their way back to faithful Christian community.
People who once hid in shame discovering the forgiveness of Christ.
And Christians growing beyond inspirational words into genuine spiritual maturity.
The Gospel must never become something people feel they have to purchase.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
Our calling is to proclaim Him faithfully.
So before you leave, return once more to that mountain outside Jerusalem.
Picture Jesus speaking to His disciples about the future.
The disciples are listening.
The world is moving toward events they cannot fully comprehend.
And Jesus says that no one knows the day or hour—not even the Son, but the Father.
For some, those words will remain a difficult theological question.
For others, they will become an invitation to study the incarnation more carefully.
But for the believer who has begun to see the whole picture, they can also become a reminder of the extraordinary humility of the Savior.
The eternal Son truly entered human life.
He did not abandon His deity.
He did not pretend to be human.
He humbled Himself.
He obeyed.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
One day He will return.
Until then, we are not called to manufacture certainty about the date.
We are called to faithfulness to the Person.
So let the scholars study.
Let the sincere questions be asked.
Let Scripture speak.
And let every discovery lead us back to the One who stands at the center of it all.
Jesus Christ.
Truly God.
Truly man.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in glory.
Coming again.
And worthy of our trust today.
The most important thing is not whether you know the hour He is coming, but whether you know the Savior who came to bring you home.
